text: Here's an island grid of heights. The Pacific touches the top and left edges, and the Atlantic touches the bottom and right edges. Water flows from a cell to a neighbor of equal or lower height. Return every cell from which water can reach both oceans.

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Just to make sure I'm understanding this correctly — flow is four-directional, downhill or flat, and a cell on an ocean edge drains straight into it. I want the cells that reach the Pacific and the Atlantic. Is that right?

Okay. The clean idea is to reverse it. Rather than ask each cell, can you flow to an ocean, I start at the ocean edges and walk inland and uphill — to neighbors of equal or greater height. Whatever I can reach that way is exactly the set of cells that can flow down to that ocean. I flood once from the Pacific edges, once from the Atlantic edges, and intersect.

Hmm, let me think about this for a sec. A naive approach would be to search from every cell and check if it reaches both oceans — that's the square of m times n. This problem reminds me of a reverse flood fill: when many starting points share one target, search backward from the target instead. Two flood fills from the borders, going uphill, then intersect the two reachable sets. One linear pass each — O of m times n.

Here's the plan. One: flood from the Pacific edges, the top row and left column, into p set. Two: flood from the Atlantic edges, the bottom row and right column, into a set — each step only goes to a neighbor at least as high. Three: collect the cells marked in both. Here, I'm using two separate visited grids to keep track of what each ocean can reach, so I can intersect them at the end. One thing worth flagging — the flood condition is greater or equal, not less or equal. Real flow is downhill, so the reversed walk goes uphill. And it includes equals, because equal-height cells share flow. There's a trade-off here. Two m by n boolean grids cost extra memory, but they buy linear time over the quadratic per-cell search. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?

Alright, let me code this up. The main function runs a DFS from every border cell: the left and top edges fill p set, the right and bottom edges fill a set. Then one scan collects every cell that's true in both. The DFS marks the cell on entry, skips out-of-bounds neighbors first, then skips anything already seen or lower than the current cell. One thing worth flagging — neighbor lower than current is the guard I continue on, which means I only recurse when the neighbor is greater or equal. Flip that comparison and the whole thing floods the wrong direction.

Let's dry-run the code with the example: the five by five grid from the problem, expected seven cells. The Pacific flood covers the top-left wedge, and the Atlantic flood covers the bottom-right wedge. The cell that shows the idea is two, two, the peak of height five in the middle: the Pacific climbs to it from the three above, and the Atlantic from the three on its right, so it's in both. Overlaying the two sets gives the seven expected cells. That matches. Corner cases: a single cell touches all four edges, so the output is zero, zero. A perfectly flat grid floods everywhere from both sides, so every cell qualifies.

Let me think about complexity here. The time complexity is O of m times n — two floods, each visiting every cell at most once, plus a linear intersection scan. The space complexity is O of m times n for the two boolean grids and the recursion stack. Oh, one more thing — the whole win is the reversal. Asking, can this cell reach the ocean, per cell is quadratic; asking, what can the ocean reach going uphill, is one linear flood per ocean. That reverse-the-search trick shows up whenever many sources share one target.

Nicely done. Three things stood out. You reversed the question — flooding from the oceans uphill instead of searching per cell, dropping it from quadratic to linear. You got the greater-or-equal condition right and explained why equal heights connect. And you kept two separate visited grids so the intersection is clean. Good work.
